awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of a Wireless Implant for Brain Neuromodulation
awd_abstract_narration:
The impact of this I-Corps project is based on the lab to market translation of a wireless neuromodulation system used in implantable medical devices. This novel system eliminates the need for a battery by using wireless power to activate the device only when needed, minimizing the need for post-implantation interventions. This solution addresses the current need for an on-board battery and/or frequent battery changes. This approach enables the development of smaller, more efficient devices focused on data acquisition and transmission, while also minimizing the size and complexity of the power-receiving components. The implantable medical device market is expected to grow significantly, with over 3 million potential patients in the U.S. by the end of the decade. This technology could benefit this patient population by improving the efficiency, safety, and longevity of implantable devices. 

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of phased-array-based simultaneous tracking, communication, and powering of an optogenetic neuromodulation implant. This implant can inhibit or excite specific genetically modified neurons using specific wavelengths of light emitted through micro light emitting diodes (LEDs). This new solution consists of a small, highly efficient, multiband antenna as a receiver (implant) antenna, an active phased-array transmitter, and a rectifier to convert the radiofrequency signal into a direct current (DC) signal. By enabling safer, battery-free medical implants, the technology reduces the need for invasive procedures, leading to better patient outcomes and lower healthcare costs. The miniaturization of the implantable devices paves the way for more accessible and portable medical solutions, fostering innovation in wearable health monitoring and personalized medicine.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Implantable neuromodulation devices stimulate or quiet specific groups of nerve cells. They are important tools for studying the brain, and they are increasingly used or explored to treat conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, epilepsy, chronic pain, and depression. Most of today’s implants depend on an on-board battery or a wire that passes through the skin. Batteries add size and weight and eventually require another surgery to replace. External wires limit movement and create a pathway for infection. This NSF I-Corps Teams project examined whether a battery-free, wireless brain implant developed in our laboratory could make the transition from the lab to the marketplace, and identified who would benefit most.

Our system powers an optogenetic implant, a tiny device that uses micro light-emitting diodes (micro-LEDs) to turn genetically targeted neurons on or off with specific colors of light. The implant has no battery. An external phased-array transmitter steers radio-frequency energy electronically toward the implant. A small, highly efficient multiband antenna on the implant captures this energy, and a rectifier converts it into usable electrical power. The same wireless link also tracks the implant’s location and carries communication. As a result, power stays focused on the implant even when the subject is moving freely.

Through the I-Corps program, our team conducted more than 200 customer discovery interviews. We spoke with neuroscience researchers, neurosurgeons and clinicians, medical device engineers and manufacturers, research-equipment suppliers, regulatory experts, investors, and government program managers. We also took part in more than 10 trade shows, conferences, and agency meetings, including TechConnect and meetings with the Office of Naval Research (ONR) and the U.S. Army. These conversations let us test our assumptions about the value of wireless power and learn what matters most to each type of customer.

Several key findings came out of this process. First, interviewees consistently said that batteries and tethers are major limitations: they restrict natural behavior in research subjects, add surgical risk, and increase cost. Second, [preclinical neuroscience research, such as studies in freely moving animals,] emerged as the most promising early market. Researchers in this market need reliable, untethered stimulation now, and the regulatory path for research tools is shorter than the path for human medical devices. Third, the path to human clinical use will require biocompatible packaging, long-term reliability data, and approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. We now understand these steps and their timelines much better. Fourth, our meetings with defense agencies revealed interest in wireless neurotechnology for research on traumatic brain injury, post-traumatic stress, and warfighter health and performance. Finally, customers said that ease of integration with existing surgical procedures and laboratory equipment is as important as technical performance. That insight is now shaping our design priorities.

Together, these findings helped the team refine its value proposition, prioritize customer segments, and define a realistic commercialization roadmap. That roadmap starts with research tools and moves toward clinical and defense applications.

Wireless, battery-free implants could reduce repeat surgeries, lower infection risk, and improve comfort and mobility for patients who rely on neuromodulation therapies. In the near term, a reliable untethered research platform can help neuroscientists study brain function in more natural conditions, which may speed discoveries about neurological and psychiatric disorders.

The project also trained 2 doctoral students and researchers in customer discovery, business model development, and technology commercialization. These skills complement their engineering expertise and prepare them for careers in the U.S. biomedical technology workforce. The team shared its work with industry, academic, and government audiences through trade shows and agency meetings, building connections with potential partners, manufacturers, and funders.

Building on what we learned through I-Corps, the team is pursuing biocompatibility testing, advanced prototyping, intellectual property protection, partnerships with device integrators and clinical collaborators, and follow-on funding such as SBIR/STTR and defense research programs. Our goal is to bring a safe, compact, and wireless neuromodulation platform first to the research community and eventually to patients.
